name: Colin Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What does your ordinary day at the accounting firm look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The hotel night audit is my first file, and there is often one refunded room that the booking list still counts as a sale. I use AI to flag the mismatch, check the original log, then prepare the accounts and tax return for review. I am 43, with a bachelor’s degree and a professional accountancy qualification; I know this work reasonably well and like the little detective part, but a hotel owner calling during family dinner wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and how often do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mae works in catering, and our children Jo and Mina are both school age. We pay a mortgage, though my salary is high for this accounting role, we have about nine months of expenses saved, and plenty of similar firms operate nearby. I use AI every day for first checks, but I compare each flag with the booking record before changing a number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hotel would still send a night audit sheet with one room missing. A little faster sorting would not change my Saturday phone call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team that faster matching is welcome when the original booking record stays visible. I use AI every day for first-pass checks, then I explain the mismatch before we file a hotel’s return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I expect my well-paid post to continue, and my partner Mae and I have around nine months of expenses saved. Plenty of accounting firms are nearby, so the mortgage does not feel at risk in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the hotel accounts and compare each AI flag with the source booking sheet. From next payday I would transfer eighty from salary into our emergency account until it covers a year of expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the job and bills. The hotel owner calling at dinner would still annoy me more than the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the checker miss recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It marked a refunded room as a second sale, but I found the cancellation in the night log. I changed the account before my manager saw the return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why build more cash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mae’s catering income varies with events, and we have two children and a mortgage. Eighty a month is new saving from my pay, not a claim that our nine months are already twelve.

say: I would welcome **faster matching** when the booking record remains visible.
I would keep a **human explanation** for each hotel account mismatch.
think: My **high pay** and nine-month reserve keep the mortgage secure.
There are **many firms** nearby if the current one changes.
do: Check **AI flags** against hotel booking sheets on current accounts.
Transfer **eighty monthly** from wages until one year is saved.
feel: I feel **calm** about my own income.
S0.quote: The hotel owner calling at dinner would still annoy me more than the software.
fieldNote: He uses AI **daily** but corrected a refunded room that the tool marked as a second sale.
His new **eighty-monthly deposits** account for variable catering income while preserving a strong buffer.

steps.text: Keep checking AI flags against hotel booking sheets
Transfer eighty monthly from salary until reserve covers one year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Room accounts are full of the writing and checking on the card. I would want to see whether the firm keeps reviewers when the tool gets faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a test on past hotel returns with known refund errors before changing our sign-off. I would tell colleagues a quicker draft is useful only if clients still get a named answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own review hours could shrink when several hotel accounts are handled by one checker. Nine months saved gives us room, but Mae’s catering income cannot reliably replace my high accounting wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my manager Talia for a paid trial on old anonymised hotel returns and compare the wrong refund entries myself. If the trial passes, I would put the approved tool into our current workflow with her sign-off; if my hours fall in the first year, I would seek a posted hotel-accounting post only with written pay, hours, and a start date covering the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about reduced paid hours despite being comfortable with the tool. I do not want a rushed setting to make a client pay twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides whether the trial passes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talia and I would count missed refunds and false flags, then sign a report on paid work time. If she refuses the trial, I would keep the current process and salary rather than install software on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave for a promising firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after it gives me a written contract with a start date and enough wage for our fixed bills. A good conversation is not a second income.

feel: I feel **anxious** about my own paid hours.
S1.quote: A good conversation is not a second income.
fieldNote: He tests **refund errors**, not just speed, and requires the manager’s paid sign-off before changing live work.
His high salary and variable partner income make **written terms** vital to a job move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years would arrive before many hotel contracts renew. Robots around 2031 would not postpone the accounting desk loss in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell clients the firm still needs a named person responsible for returns when AGI prepares them in 2028. I would not tell staff that a fast pilot can guarantee a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I expect most of our hotel preparation fees to vanish and my post to go. Nine months of savings would buy search time, but Mae’s event income and our mortgage make a long gap risky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would defer the planned larger car and move its monthly budget into job-loss cash. If my post ends in the first year after 2028, I would apply to posted hotel finance supervisor roles only with written pay, hours, and a start date covering our mortgage; I would keep my present salary until a real offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect to lose the wage we built the mortgage around. I can search carefully. A reserve is not a guarantee of a new vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a finance supervisor role last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might not; AGI can do screen checks there too. I would treat an actual paid offer as a bridge, not a shelter from the same technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mae?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Mae that the current car can keep taking the children to school. We would delay the bigger one until my salary is certain.

I would say **2031 robots** do not delay the hotel accounts shock.
think: I expect my **hotel accounts post** to go when AGI replaces preparation and checks.

feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely loss of my salary.
S2.quote: A reserve is not a guarantee of a new vacancy.
fieldNote: He expects a **2028 desk loss**, three years before capable hands-on robots arrive.
The larger-car budget becomes **new cash saving** while hotel finance remains only a possible paid bridge.

steps.text: Defer larger car and deposit its monthly budget into job-loss cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me find out whether hotels still pay for someone to explain a tax discrepancy. I would test that while employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the firm to give reviewers paid time to meet hotel owners before 2031, not only a screen full of AI flags. AGI reaches desk work then; robots around 2034 are later for hotel cleaning and service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still think the routine return fees could fall, but five years lets me build a record of resolving owner questions. I would want a budgeted client role before treating those conversations as future income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the professional body’s short hotel-tax update course if Talia approves paid time and the firm pays its fee, then lead one owner meeting quarterly only if she assigns it. I would transfer eighty monthly from salary into cash; in the first year after 2031 I would take a posted client-finance role only with written pay, hours, and a start date covering our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the long-term post, though I can keep earning while I test client demand. Five years is enough to build evidence, not certainty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course fee is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use free professional tax notes and keep checking the current hotel accounts while paid. I would not spend the household reserve on a certificate without a funded role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the owner meetings be paid work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Talia assigns them on my paid schedule. I would not call a lunchtime favour a path to a new salary.

I would separate **2031 desk change** from later 2034 robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would put both children further along in school. I could build assets without pretending hotel accounts stay the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell clients the firm has a decade to teach reviewers how to question AI and give owners a named answer. AGI reaches hotel accounts desks in 2036, while robots enter hands-on work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect ordinary return fees to fall eventually, but my current pay and nine-month reserve keep the next few years secure. I could have a longer cash runway and a proven client role by 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep reviewing the hotel accounts and transfer eighty monthly from salary until the reserve covers eighteen months. I would lead paid owner meetings only if Talia assigns them; if my review post contracts in the first year after 2036, I would take a posted client-finance role only with written pay, hours, and a start date covering the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about later work, but not this year’s bills. Ten years lets me judge a real client role before leaving a good wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you invest in a hotel yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, one hotel is too large a bet for our family. I would keep the new deposits in cash until the job picture is clearer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children Jo and Mina to learn how to check a number and explain it to someone else. A fast answer is only useful if you can defend it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the hotel accounts post that supports our mortgage could vanish before a new salary begins. A clear staff plan, paid hotel-tax learning, and a written job offer would help. I would keep the current job while it still pays and require an actual start date elsewhere before resigning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what happens when a hotel guest gets charged twice. A wrong booking entry can become a real argument at reception before anyone sees the tax return. I want clients to see the source of every correction.

headlineQuote: A wrong booking entry can become a real argument at reception before anyone sees the tax return.
portrait: Colin is a **43-year-old** experienced accountant with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification who checks hotel returns.
He has **high pay**, nine months saved, a catering partner, two school-age children, and a mortgage.
He uses **AI daily** to find mismatches, then checks booking logs before changing accounts.
The **2028** desk shock alarms him despite cash; hotel finance work is a conditional paid bridge.
Longer warning allows **funded hotel-tax learning**, assigned owner meetings, and new monthly cash deposits.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his hotel accounts wage before another salary starts.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a clear **staff plan**, paid hotel-tax learning, and a written offer with a start date.
